examples.title: Confidence interval for one mean
examples.prompt: Ten BME 423 students have a mean heart rate of 67 beats/min with a sample SD of 9 beats/min. Find the 95% confidence interval for the population mean heart rate \(\mu_{HR}\).

steps.say: The SD of 9 beats/min is divided by the square root of 10. So the mean of ten students is uncertain by about 2.846 beats/min.
Row 9 and the two-tailed 0.05 column of the t table give 2.262. That column already holds both tails, so it is not halved again.
The margin is the cutoff times the standard error, about 6.44 beats/min. Taking it off 67 gives the lower end and adding it gives the upper end.
We are 95% confident that the mean heart rate of all BME 423 students is between about 60.6 and 73.4 beats/min. This range is for the mean, not for single students.

examples.title: Confidence interval for a difference of two means
examples.prompt: Daily urine production is compared between a diuretic group and a placebo group. Assume Normal responses with a common variance. Find the 95% confidence interval for \(\mu_{\mathrm{diuretic}}-\mu_{\mathrm{placebo}}\).

steps.say: Diuretic minus placebo is 220 mL/day. This order is kept to the end so the sign of the interval keeps its meaning.
Each variance is weighted by its own 9 degrees of freedom before pooling. The pooled variance then gives a standard error of about 89.87 mL/day.
Row 18 and the two-tailed 0.05 column of the t table give 2.101.
The margin is about 188.8 mL/day. It is taken off and added to the difference of 220 mL/day.
work: (\bar x_1-\bar x_2)\pm t_c\, s_{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}

steps.say: We are 95% confident that the diuretic raises mean urine production by between about 31 and 409 mL/day. Zero is outside the interval, so the diuretic does change urine production.

examples.title: Confidence interval for one proportion
examples.prompt: A survey asked college students “Did you take a non-prescribed stimulant in the last year?” Of the 500 students who responded, 177 said yes. Find the 95% confidence interval for the population proportion and decide whether it differs from 0.5.

steps.say: 177 of the 500 students said yes. So the sample proportion is 0.354.
The proportion times one minus the proportion is divided by 500. The square root gives a standard error of about 0.0214.
The infinity row and the 0.05 column of the t table give 1.96. So the interval runs from about 0.312 to 0.396.
One half lies above the whole interval. So the proportion of students who took a stimulant differs from 0.5 at the 0.05 level, and it is lower.

examples.title: Confidence interval for a difference of two proportions
examples.prompt: A trial records thrombosis with placebo and with aspirin. Find the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the probability of thrombosis, placebo minus aspirin, using the pooled standard error.

steps.say: Group 1 is placebo and group 2 is aspirin. The difference is placebo minus aspirin, so a positive value means more thrombosis with placebo.
The counts and the sizes are added first to get the pooled proportion. That pooled value goes into the standard error, which is about 0.1515.
Proportions use the Normal distribution, so the cutoff comes from the infinity row of the t table in the 0.05 column.
The margin is about 0.297. So the interval runs from about 0.107 to 0.701.
work: (\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm z_c\, s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}

steps.say: With 95% confidence, aspirin lowers the chance of thrombosis by about 10.7 to 70.1 percentage points compared with placebo. Zero is outside, so the two probabilities differ.

examples.title: Decide significance from intervals only
examples.prompt: Six-month survival after heart-transplant surgery is compared between two ways of transporting the heart. Find the 95% and 99% confidence intervals for the difference in the proportion alive at 6 months. Using only these intervals, is the difference significant with \(P<0.05\)? With \(P<0.01\)? State how you reached each conclusion.

steps.say: The 95% interval uses the pooled standard error and the cutoff 1.96. It runs from about 0.035 to 0.259, so it does not contain zero.
Zero is outside the 95% interval, so a difference of zero is not a believable value. The difference in survival is significant with P less than 0.05.
The 99% interval uses 2.5758 from the infinity row and the 0.01 column. Its lower end sits just below zero, so the difference is not significant with P less than 0.01.
This is a difference of two proportions, so the null value is zero and not one half. A single proportion would be checked against its own reference value instead.
The 95% interval leaves out zero, so P is below 0.05. The wider 99% interval just includes zero, so P is not below 0.01. The higher survival with warm transport is significant at the 0.05 level only.
